profile.name: Adil Osman
profile.title: Data Engineer | Analytics Engineer | Data Scientist
profile.education: First Class BSc in Data Science & Computing — Birkbeck, University of London
profile.bio: London-based data professional with professional experience as a Junior Data Engineer at Somalis in Tech and Junior Data Analyst at HQ Analytics (Dubai). Designs reliable, observable data pipelines and analytics-ready warehouse systems. Experience spans real-time ingestion, CDC architectures, lakehouses, and dbt-driven transformations across finance, sports, transport, and environmental sectors.
profile.elevatorPitch: I'm Adil, a London-based data engineer with a First Class BSc from Birkbeck. Most recently I was a Junior Data Engineer at Somalis in Tech where I built production pipelines with Python, SQL, dbt, and Airflow — improving data freshness from 6 hours to 45 minutes and mentoring 12 early-career candidates. Before that, I was a Data Analyst at HQ Analytics in Dubai where I built Power BI dashboards, reduced data defects by 30%, and contributed to an 8% cut in logistics costs. I also created a TfL Travel App for London students and commuters as a community project. My portfolio spans CDC streaming, lakehouses, analytics warehouses, and ML platforms.

Improved data freshness from 6 hours to 45 minutes (87% improvement)

coreTips.title: Lead with the number, then the story
coreTips.body: You have unusually concrete metrics for someone early in their career. Open an answer with '87%' or '30%' and the interviewer leans in — then spend the rest of the answer earning it. Never leave a result unquantified when you have the figure.

coreTips.title: Every answer lands on a real project
coreTips.body: Abstract knowledge sounds rehearsed; a named system sounds like experience. TfL for batch and orchestration, StreamShop for streaming and CDC, F1 RaceOps and Premier League for modelling, HQ Analytics for stakeholders. Pick one before you start talking.

coreTips.title: Say 'I', credit the team separately
coreTips.body: Interviewers are hiring you, not your team. Describe your decisions and your code in the first person, then give credit explicitly at the end. 'We' throughout an answer makes your contribution impossible to assess.

coreTips.title: Clarify before you solve
coreTips.body: On any design or SQL question, ask what the source is, what the volume is, what the SLA is, and who consumes it. Jumping straight to tools is the single most common failure mode in data interviews — and asking costs you fifteen seconds.

coreTips.title: Own the gaps out loud
coreTips.body: You have not run Spark at petabyte scale or managed a large cloud estate. Say so plainly, then pivot to how you learned dbt, Debezium, and ClickHouse from scratch. Confident honesty reads as senior; bluffing gets caught in the follow-up.

coreTips.title: Finish with what you would do next
coreTips.body: Close technical answers with the improvement you did not have time for. It signals that you know the difference between shipped and finished, which is exactly what an interviewer is trying to work out.

tips: Have the two-minute version of your background ready: Birkbeck First, Somalis in Tech, HQ Analytics, portfolio, what you want next.
Read the company's engineering blog and name their stack back to them. Specifics separate you from the pile.
Expect surface-level technical screening — SQL fundamentals and 'tell me about a project'. Depth comes later.
Bring three questions about the team's data challenges. Not perks.
Narrate before you type. Silence during live coding reads as being stuck, even when you are thinking.
Window functions, CTEs and joins are near-certain. Rehearse ROW_NUMBER deduplication until it is muscle memory.
Expect 'why did you choose X over Y' — have the DuckDB-over-Postgres and Redpanda-over-Kafka reasoning ready.
If you do not know something, say what you would read and how you would test it.
This round crosses domains — expect data quality tangled up with stakeholder communication.
Scenario questions ('the pipeline breaks at 2am before a board meeting') are testing composure and process, not trivia.
Talk about operating systems, not just building them: alerting, ownership, runbooks, backfills.
Have one example of a technical disagreement you resolved with evidence rather than seniority.
Read the brief twice and underline every requirement. Missing a stated requirement fails more take-homes than weak code does.
Time-box to the stated hours. Over-engineering signals poor prioritisation, not enthusiasm.
Ship a README with your approach, assumptions, and how to run it — plus a few tests on the logic that matters.
End with a 'what I would do next' section. It is the cheapest seniority signal in the whole submission.
Your skills are already validated by this point. Shift from 'I can do the work' to 'I am the right person for this team'.
Know your London market range and say it without flinching, then note you are flexible on the total package.
Reference specific conversations from earlier rounds. It shows you were listening, not performing.
Ask how success is measured at six months, and about the decision timeline.

questions.question: Tell me about yourself.
questions.answer: I'm a data engineer based in London with a First Class BSc in Data Science and Computing from Birkbeck. Most recently I spent about a year and a half as a Junior Data Engineer at Somalis in Tech, building production pipelines in Python, SQL, dbt and Airflow — the headline result there was taking data freshness from six hours down to forty-five minutes while holding 95% on-time SLA compliance. Alongside that I mentored around twelve early-career engineers. Before that I was a Junior Data Analyst at HQ Analytics in Dubai, where I cut data defects by 30% and built Power BI dashboards for twenty-five-odd users across operations. Outside work I've built a portfolio around the things I want to do more of — a CDC streaming pipeline with Debezium and ClickHouse, a few dbt warehouses, and a real-time lakehouse on TfL data. What I'm looking for now is a team where I can own reliable pipelines end to end.
questions.evidence: Somalis in Tech · HQ Analytics · 87% freshness · 12 mentees
questions.watchOut: Do not list all ten portfolio projects. Name two at most and stop — the interviewer will ask about the ones they care about.

questions.question: What are you looking for in your next role? / Why are you leaving?
questions.answer: I want to go deeper on production ownership. At Somalis in Tech I built and ran pipelines, but the scale was what a small team needs — I want to work on systems where reliability is genuinely hard, where there are real SLAs and real consequences when a pipeline is late. I'd also like to be the more junior person in a strong team for a while. I've spent a lot of the last year mentoring, which I loved, but I learn fastest when I'm the one having my design decisions challenged. Concretely: somewhere using dbt and a proper orchestrator, with a team that treats data quality as part of the build rather than something you bolt on afterwards. That's the part of the work I care most about.
questions.evidence: Somalis in Tech · mentoring 12 engineers
questions.watchOut: Never frame it as escaping something. Growth-forward, specific, and never critical of a former employer.

questions.question: What interests you about this role / company?
questions.answer: Building the TfL Travel App taught me something that stuck. It started because a student on the mentorship programme asked how they'd actually know when their bus was coming — and the gap between 'it works' and 'it helps someone' turned out to be most of the engineering. That's the kind of data work I want to keep doing: systems where somebody downstream is genuinely better off. From what I've read about your stack and the problems your team is solving, that's what this role is — pipelines with real consumers, not reporting for its own sake. I'm also drawn to the tooling overlap; I've been working with dbt and Airflow daily and I'd rather go deeper on that than start again somewhere else.
questions.evidence: TfL Travel App · Somalis in Tech
questions.watchOut: This answer must be re-tailored per company. Replace the last two sentences with something specific you actually read about them.

questions.question: Walk me through your most recent role and the impact you had.
questions.answer: At Somalis in Tech I was the Junior Data Engineer on a small team, and my main piece of work was the TfL data platform. When I picked it up, data was landing roughly every six hours through a manual process, which meant nothing built on it could be close to real time. I rebuilt it as a four-layer pipeline: Airflow polling the TfL Unified API every three minutes into date and hour partitioned Parquet, dbt transforming through staging, intermediate and marts, and Great Expectations validating quality at the staging boundary. That took freshness to forty-five minutes — an 87% improvement — and we held 95% on-time SLA compliance with sub-sixty-minute latency. It also cut manual reporting by about 65%, because reports that people had been assembling by hand became marts. And because it was a community organisation, the pipeline doubled as the teaching platform for the twelve engineers I was mentoring.
questions.evidence: Somalis in Tech · 87% freshness · 95% SLA · 65% less manual reporting
questions.watchOut: Do not skip the 'before' state. The 87% only means something once they know it was six hours and manual.

questions.question: You improved data freshness from six hours to forty-five minutes. How?
questions.answer: Three changes, in order of impact. First, the ingestion was manual and batch — I moved it to Airflow polling the TfL Unified API on a three-minute schedule, writing straight into date and hour partitioned Parquet, so raw data was always current. Second, the transformations were full-refresh, so every run reprocessed everything and got slower as the dataset grew. I moved the heavy models to incremental dbt materialisations keyed on the partition, so a run only touches new data. Third, and this was the one I didn't expect, a lot of the six hours was waiting for a human to notice a failure. I added Great Expectations checks at staging plus OpenLineage so a break surfaced immediately with the affected downstream models attached, instead of being discovered when someone's dashboard looked wrong. Forty-five minutes is what's left, and most of it is the polling interval by design — hammering the API harder would have hit rate limits for no real benefit.
questions.evidence: TfL Travel App · Airflow · dbt incremental · Great Expectations · OpenLineage
questions.watchOut: The third point is the strongest one because it is about operations, not code. Do not rush it.

questions.question: Tell me about your analyst experience.
questions.answer: I spent nine months as a Junior Data Analyst at HQ Analytics in Dubai, working remotely with their operations teams. The core of it was multi-source preprocessing — data arriving from several systems with inconsistent keys, formats and definitions. I built a standardised cleaning and validation step in front of the reporting layer, which brought data defects down by about 30%. The bigger win was turnaround: requests had been taking three days because every one started from raw data, and by building reusable Power BI dashboards for twenty-five-plus users I got most of it to same-day, roughly a 67% improvement. Out of the exploratory work I put forward twelve-odd concrete recommendations, and the ones the business acted on contributed to an 8% reduction in logistics costs and a 12% improvement in on-time delivery. That role is where I learned that the analysis is the easy part — getting people to trust and use it is the job.
questions.evidence: HQ Analytics · 30% fewer defects · 67% faster turnaround · 8% cost reduction
questions.watchOut: For a DE role, land on what the analyst experience gives you now: you know what your consumers actually need.

questions.question: What's the most technically challenging thing you've built?
structure: What changed in how you think
questions.answer: StreamShop, my CDC analytics pipeline. It captures changes from a PostgreSQL write-ahead log with Debezium, publishes them to Redpanda, and a Python consumer lands them in ClickHouse, where dbt models them into current-state and SCD2 history tables. The hard part wasn't wiring it together — it was everything that happens when the happy path stops. Ordering: events for the same key have to be applied in sequence, so the consumer is keyed and idempotent rather than just appending. Deletes: a CDC delete isn't a row you can ignore, so I carry a _deleted flag through to the models instead of losing history. Schema changes: I put Avro and a schema registry in front of the topics so a producer change is caught as a contract violation rather than silently corrupting downstream tables. And I implemented the outbox pattern so domain events are published in the same transaction as the state change, which removes the dual-write problem entirely. It's the project where I stopped thinking about pipelines as data movement and started thinking about them as guarantees.
questions.evidence: StreamShop CDC · Debezium · Redpanda · ClickHouse · SCD2 · outbox
questions.watchOut: The last sentence is the point of the whole answer. Do not let the tool list eat the time you need for it.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you mentored or led others.
questions.answer: At Somalis in Tech I mentored about twelve early-career data engineers, and I structured it around four modules — API ingestion, data modelling, data quality, and pipeline orchestration — using the TfL platform as the live teaching system rather than toy exercises. The thing I got wrong at the start was demonstrating too much. I'd walk through my solution, everyone would nod, and then nobody could reproduce it. So I switched to giving them a broken pipeline and letting them diagnose it, which was slower and much more uncomfortable, and it worked — several of them went on to build their own lakehouses afterwards. What I took from it is that explaining something well is a completely different skill from doing it well, and the second one made me better at the first. My design docs and PR descriptions got a lot clearer once I'd spent a year having to justify decisions to people who would immediately ask why.
questions.evidence: Somalis in Tech · 12 mentees · 4 modules · TfL platform
questions.watchOut: Include the thing you got wrong. A mentoring story with no mistake in it sounds like a brochure.

questions.question: Explain window functions and when you'd use one.
questions.answer: A window function computes across a set of related rows without collapsing them, which is the key difference from GROUP BY — you keep row-level output and gain context. I reach for them whenever I need each row plus something about its neighbours: ranking, deduplication, running totals, or comparing a row to the previous one. The one I use most is deduplication. To get the latest status per application I'd write ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY application_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC, event_id DESC) and filter to row number one. The second ordering column matters — with timestamps at second granularity you get ties, and without a tiebreaker the result is non-deterministic, which is a genuinely nasty bug because it passes tests intermittently. I use LAG for day-over-day comparisons and SUM with an unbounded preceding frame for cumulative totals. In F1 RaceOps I use them heavily for ranking pit stop performance within a race.
questions.evidence: F1 RaceOps · driver and pit stop ranking
questions.watchOut: Say the tiebreaker point out loud. It is the detail that separates someone who has used these in production from someone who has read about them.

questions.question: A dashboard query is slow. How do you investigate?
questions.answer: I'd reproduce and measure before changing anything, because the most common mistake here is guessing at an index. First I check whether it's actually the query or the surrounding context — concurrency, a cold cache, or a dashboard firing twelve queries where one would do. Then I read the execution plan and look for the expensive step: a full scan where I expected a partition prune, a nested loop over something large, a spill, or a shuffle in a distributed engine. From there the fixes go in rough order of payoff. Reduce data scanned first — push filters earlier, stop selecting columns nobody uses, make sure partition and cluster keys line up with how the dashboard actually filters. Then fix joins, checking key cardinality and whether a broadcast is appropriate. Indexing or clustering comes after that, and materialising the result comes last, because it's the option that adds a freshness obligation. On the Premier League warehouse in BigQuery, most of my cost savings came from partition pruning and dropping columns, not from anything clever.
questions.evidence: Premier League warehouse · BigQuery partition pruning
questions.watchOut: Lead with 'measure first'. Candidates who open by suggesting an index lose the point immediately.

questions.question: How would you handle a value that changes over time — say a customer's address?
questions.answer: It depends on whether anyone needs to ask questions about the past. If not, a Type 1 overwrite is fine and much cheaper — people over-engineer this. But the moment someone wants to know what a metric looked like at the time, you need Type 2: each version becomes a row with valid_from and valid_to timestamps and a current flag, and facts join on the key plus the event date falling inside that window. I've implemented this twice. In StreamShop it's built on the CDC stream in ClickHouse with _version and _deleted fields, so a delete closes the current record rather than removing history. In F1 RaceOps I used dbt snapshots, which handle the same pattern declaratively. The two things that bite you are late-arriving changes, where a new version turns up out of order and you have to reopen and re-close an interval, and joins that forget the date predicate — those silently fan out and inflate every downstream number.
questions.evidence: StreamShop CDC · SCD2 in ClickHouse · F1 RaceOps · dbt snapshots
questions.watchOut: Start with 'does anyone need history' — recommending Type 2 unconditionally is the wrong instinct.

questions.question: How would you clean a messy dataset — duplicate IDs, inconsistent dates, missing values?
structure: Missing values are a business call
questions.answer: I'd profile before touching anything, because the fix depends on the scale of the problem — how many rows are affected, whether the bad rows cluster in one source or one date range. Then I work in a fixed order. Parse dates explicitly with to_datetime and errors set to coerce, then count what failed to parse rather than letting it disappear. Standardise the categorical fields next, because inconsistent casing and whitespace are what make deduplication miss. Then deduplicate on a stable key with an explicit rule for which row wins — usually the most recent by update timestamp — not just drop_duplicates and hope. Missing values are a business decision, not a technical one: forward-fill is right for a sensor reading, wrong for a transaction amount, so I ask rather than assume. And I finish with assertions and a summary of exactly how many rows were changed or dropped. At HQ Analytics that discipline is where the 30% defect reduction came from — the audit trail is what made people trust the numbers.
questions.evidence: HQ Analytics · 30% defect reduction · TfL and London Air ingestion
questions.watchOut: The 'blind dropna' trap is the one they are testing for. Make the missing-value policy explicitly a business question.

questions.question: How do you handle API rate limits and flaky external dependencies?
questions.answer: This was a real constraint on the TfL Travel App, not a hypothetical. The Unified API has rate limits and I needed three-minute freshness across a lot of stops, so uniform polling wasn't going to fit in the budget. I moved to priority-based polling: high-traffic stops refresh on the fast cadence, quieter ones back off, and the priority is derived from actual usage rather than set by hand. When we did approach the limit, the pipeline degraded gracefully to cached data with the staleness surfaced to the consumer, instead of failing the run — a slightly old arrival time is useful, an error page isn't. Underneath that, the standard defences: retries with exponential backoff and jitter, timeouts on everything, and a circuit breaker so a sustained outage doesn't have Airflow retrying into a wall for an hour. And the raw layer stores the unmodified response, so if I discover a parsing bug next week I can reprocess history without re-hitting the API.
questions.evidence: TfL Travel App · priority polling · graceful degradation · immutable raw layer
questions.watchOut: The graceful-degradation choice is the interesting part — it is a product decision, not just an engineering one.

questions.question: Design a data pipeline from scratch.
questions.answer: I'd ask four questions before drawing anything: what's the source and can I control it, where does the data need to land, what's the freshness SLA, and what's the volume and growth. Those four answers determine most of the design. Assuming a typical case — an API source, analytics consumers, hourly freshness — I'd land raw responses immutably first, partitioned by date and hour, and never transform on the way in. That raw layer is what lets you reprocess when you find a bug, and you always find a bug. Orchestration in Airflow with idempotent tasks, so a rerun of any partition produces the same result and a backfill is just a rerun over a range. Transformation in dbt through staging, intermediate and marts, incremental where volume justifies the complexity and not before. Quality checks at the staging boundary so bad data stops before it reaches anything anyone looks at, plus freshness and volume monitoring with a named owner for alerts. That's the shape of both the TfL and London Air Quality pipelines.
questions.evidence: TfL Lakehouse · London Air Quality · Airflow · dbt medallion
questions.watchOut: Ask the four questions out loud even if they hand you the answers. The asking is what is being scored.

questions.question: Design a CDC pipeline from Postgres into an analytics database.
questions.answer: I've built exactly this, so I'll describe what I did and where the sharp edges were. Debezium reads the PostgreSQL write-ahead log and publishes change events to Redpanda — which is Kafka-compatible but a single binary, so it was far easier to run locally and in CI. A Python consumer lands events in ClickHouse, and dbt models them into both a current-state table and an SCD2 history table, because those serve different questions. The parts that need care: ordering has to be preserved per key, so partitioning is by primary key and the consumer is idempotent on key plus log sequence number. Deletes must be first-class — I carry a _deleted flag rather than dropping rows, otherwise you lose the fact that something was deleted, which is often the interesting event. Schema evolution goes through Avro and a schema registry so a producer change fails as a contract violation instead of corrupting downstream tables. And there's a replay path from a snapshot plus the log, because a consumer bug that you can't reprocess your way out of is a very bad afternoon.
questions.evidence: StreamShop CDC · Debezium · Redpanda · ClickHouse · Avro registry
questions.watchOut: Say why Redpanda over Kafka — operational simplicity for the scale you needed. Tool choices need reasons.

questions.question: Batch or streaming — how do you decide?
questions.answer: I decide on whether a decision changes with the freshness. If nobody acts differently on data that's five minutes old versus six hours old, streaming is cost and complexity you're paying for nothing. TfL was genuinely real-time-shaped — an arrival prediction is worthless if it's an hour stale — so that pipeline polls every three minutes. StreamShop was streaming because CDC is inherently event-driven; you're reading a log of changes, and batching that back up throws away the ordering you were given for free. But the F1 and Premier League warehouses are batch, because nobody needs last night's race analysed within seconds. The other half of the answer is operational: streaming systems fail differently. Backfills are harder, exactly-once is expensive, and you need people who can debug a consumer lag at 3am. I'd rather run a well-monitored hourly batch than a streaming pipeline nobody on the team can operate.
questions.evidence: TfL (3-min) · StreamShop (CDC streaming) · F1 and Premier League (batch)
questions.watchOut: Having built both is your advantage here. Name a project on each side of the line.

questions.question: How do you handle late-arriving data?
questions.answer: The root cause is usually treating yesterday's partition as final when it isn't. So the first thing I do is separate event time from processing time and keep both, because you can't reason about lateness without them. Then I define a lookback window based on how late data actually arrives — measure it, don't guess — and reprocess that window on every run rather than only the newest partition. That only works if the pipeline is idempotent, which is why I merge on stable keys instead of appending. Past the lookback window, late data becomes an explicit restatement with a backfill, not a silent correction, because a number that quietly changes after people have quoted it destroys trust faster than a number that was late. And I monitor it: if the volume of late-arriving records shifts, that's usually an upstream problem worth chasing before it becomes a metrics problem.
questions.evidence: TfL and London Air Quality · partitioned backfills
questions.watchOut: The 'silently changing numbers destroy trust' point is a maturity signal. Include it.

questions.question: How do you ensure data quality in your pipelines?
questions.answer: I build it in at layers rather than bolting a checker on the end, because by the time you're validating the output you've already lost the ability to say where it broke. At ingestion I validate structure and contract — in StreamShop that's Avro against a schema registry, so a producer change is rejected rather than absorbed. At staging I check semantics with Great Expectations: nullability on the fields that matter, and range checks on things I know the bounds of, like time-to-station on the TfL data, which can't be negative and shouldn't be six hours. In the transformation layer, dbt tests on uniqueness, not-null, accepted values and relationships run on every model, so a broken join surfaces as a failing test rather than a duplicated row count. Then freshness and volume monitoring above all of it, plus OpenLineage into Marquez so when something does fail I can see exactly which downstream models are affected instead of guessing. The principle is that checks belong where the failure happens, not where you notice it.
questions.evidence: StreamShop (Avro) · TfL and London Air (Great Expectations) · dbt tests · OpenLineage
questions.watchOut: Give a specific expectation, not just the tool name. 'Time-to-station cannot be negative' proves you wrote them.

questions.question: An upstream API changes its schema without warning. What happens?
questions.answer: In my pipelines the raw layer survives it, because I store the response unmodified — so nothing is lost even if everything downstream fails. Staging is where it breaks, deliberately: I use explicit column selection rather than select-star, so a renamed or dropped field fails loudly at the boundary instead of propagating nulls into marts that people are looking at. That's the whole design decision — fail early and visibly, because a pipeline that silently produces wrong numbers is far worse than one that stops. The dbt tests catch the second-order effects: a schema change that doesn't break parsing but breaks a join shows up as a uniqueness or relationship failure. Then it's a normal incident — assess blast radius via lineage, communicate to whoever consumes the affected marts before they notice themselves, fix staging, and reprocess from raw. Afterwards I'd add an expectation for that specific field, because upstreams that change once change again.
questions.evidence: TfL Travel App · immutable raw · explicit staging columns · dbt tests
questions.watchOut: 'Fail loudly rather than propagate nulls' is the sentence they are listening for.

questions.question: How would you structure a dbt project from scratch?
questions.answer: Three layers, and the discipline is about what's allowed in each. Staging does one thing per source — rename to consistent conventions, cast types, light cleaning, no business logic and no joins. One staging model per source table, materialised as views because they're cheap and always current. Intermediate is where reusable joins and shared logic live, so a business rule that appears in five marts is defined once and referenced, not copy-pasted — that's the layer people skip and then regret. Marts are business-facing entities and metrics, named for what a stakeholder would call them rather than what the source system calls them. Tests at every layer, with the strictest at staging where it's cheapest to catch things. On materialisation I default to views, move to tables when query time hurts, and only go incremental when volume genuinely justifies the extra complexity, because incremental models are where the subtle bugs live. That's the structure in F1 RaceOps, Premier League and the TfL pipeline.
questions.evidence: F1 RaceOps · Premier League · TfL · 3-layer dbt
questions.watchOut: The 'intermediate layer is the one people skip' observation shows you have maintained a project, not just built one.

questions.question: How would you model a new domain for analytics?
questions.answer: I start from the questions, not the tables. What decisions does this data need to support, and what's the grain of each one — because getting the grain wrong is the mistake you can't fix later without a rewrite. Then I identify the business processes, which become facts, and the things you slice by, which become dimensions. That's a star schema, and I default to it for analytics because it's the shape BI tools and analysts expect; the join is predictable and the mental model is teachable. F1 RaceOps is a good example — nine dimensions around race, driver, constructor, circuit and so on, with facts at lap and pit-stop grain, which means questions about pit stop performance and questions about season standings both have a natural home. Where a dimension changes over time and history matters, that becomes SCD2. I'd denormalise into a wide table if there's a specific dashboard that needs it and the joins are measurably hurting — but as an addition on top, not instead of the star.
questions.evidence: F1 RaceOps · 9 dimensions · lap and pit-stop grain
questions.watchOut: Say 'grain' early and explicitly. It is the vocabulary that signals you have done this properly.

questions.question: How do you explain a complex data issue to a non-technical stakeholder?
questions.answer: I lead with impact and skip the mechanism unless they ask. At HQ Analytics a dashboard the operations team relied on was showing inflated figures, and the cause was a join fanning out because a source had started sending duplicate records. Nobody needed the word 'fan-out'. What I said was: some deliveries are being counted more than once, it affects these three numbers and not the others, the totals are too high by roughly this much, we've stopped it happening from this morning, and the corrected history will be in by tomorrow. Then I offered the detail to anyone who wanted it. Three things I try to always do — say what's affected and equally clearly what isn't, because uncertainty spreads further than the actual problem; give a time, even a rough one, because 'we're looking into it' with no horizon is what makes people escalate; and follow up in writing so they can forward it without having to re-explain it themselves.
questions.evidence: HQ Analytics · 25+ dashboard users · operations teams
questions.watchOut: The 'say what is not affected' point is unusually good. Do not lose it at the end of the answer.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical approach.
structure: Why you thought it was wrong
questions.answer: On the Premier League warehouse the plan was to materialise almost everything as tables in BigQuery, for speed. I thought the cost profile was wrong for how the data was actually queried — most models were hit occasionally, and we'd be paying storage and rebuild cost on everything to make a handful of queries faster. Rather than argue it in the abstract, I built both. I measured query time and cost across a representative set of queries, and it showed that views were fine for most models and materialising the three heaviest got nearly all the benefit for a fraction of the cost. That settled it in about ten minutes, and I'd rather have spent an afternoon on evidence than a week on opinions. The thing I'd carry into any team: disagreeing well is mostly about converting the disagreement into something measurable. If you can't measure it, the disagreement is about values, and then you should say that explicitly and defer to whoever owns the decision.
questions.evidence: Premier League warehouse · BigQuery materialisation and cost
questions.watchOut: The closing principle is what elevates this from a story to a way of working. Land it.

questions.question: Tell me about a time something went wrong.
structure: What broke and who felt it
questions.answer: Early on with the TfL pipeline I hit rate limits during a busy period and the run failed, which meant no fresh arrival data for a stretch of the morning — for an app whose entire value is knowing when your bus is coming. The immediate cause was uniform polling: I was refreshing every stop at the same cadence regardless of whether anyone used it, so I was spending the API budget on stops nobody queried. I fixed the cause with priority-based polling driven by actual usage. But the more important fix was the design assumption underneath it: the pipeline treated an API failure as a run failure, when the honest behaviour is to degrade — serve cached data with the staleness visible, because slightly old is useful and nothing is not. So I added graceful degradation, plus alerting on approaching the limit rather than hitting it. What I took from it is that resilience is mostly about deciding in advance what the system should do when it can't do the ideal thing.
questions.evidence: TfL Travel App · rate limits · priority polling · graceful degradation
questions.watchOut: Give the user-visible consequence before the technical cause. Owning the impact is the whole point of the question.

questions.question: Tell me about a problem nobody else had noticed.
questions.answer: A student on the mentorship programme asked me how they'd actually know when their bus was coming. It was a throwaway question, but it pointed at something real: TfL publishes excellent open data, and none of it was reaching the students in a form they'd use. Everyone had accepted that as normal. I checked whether it was a real gap — asked around, and the pattern held — then built the TfL Travel App around three things people said they'd actually use: live arrival predictions, disruption alerts, and historical reliability. The third one surprised me. I'd assumed real-time was the whole product, but what students valued most was knowing which routes were consistently unreliable, because that changes how you plan rather than how you wait. It ended up as a real platform — forty-five-minute freshness, 65% less manual reporting, and the teaching system for twelve engineers. The lesson I keep is that the interesting problems usually arrive as an offhand question from someone who doesn't know it's a problem.
questions.evidence: TfL Travel App · Somalis in Tech · 3 data products
questions.watchOut: The surprise — historical reliability beating real-time — is what makes this sound true rather than rehearsed.

questions.question: Walk us through your take-home solution.
questions.answer: I'd start with how I read the brief, because most of the interesting decisions are interpretation rather than code — here's what I understood the requirement to be, here are the ambiguities I found, and here's the assumption I made on each and why. Then the architecture at a high level before any code: the shape, and the one or two decisions that determined it. Then the trade-offs, explicitly framed against the time box — what I chose to do properly, what I chose to do simply, and why that split. I'd show the tests, and I'd be specific that they cover the logic that matters rather than claiming coverage I don't have. Then what I'd do with more time, in priority order, which is usually where I'd want the conversation to go anyway. And I'd flag anything I'm not confident about myself before they find it — it turns a potential gotcha into a discussion, and it's a much better use of the room.
questions.evidence: Applies to any submission · mirrors your README structure
questions.watchOut: Do not open by demoing code. Interpretation and trade-offs are what is being assessed.

questions.question: What would you do in your first 90 days?
questions.answer: First thirty days I'd be trying to build an accurate map: what the pipelines are, what depends on what, where the lineage actually goes as opposed to where the docs say it goes, what the SLAs are, who consumes what, and where the team's recurring pain is. I'd also want to know what breaks most often, because that tells you more about a data platform than any architecture diagram. I'd expect to ship something small and useful in that window — a test, a fix, a piece of documentation — mostly to learn the deployment path end to end. By sixty days I'd want to be delivering scoped work in the existing systems and taking on-call or review responsibility, contributing without needing much supervision. By ninety I'd want to own something measurable: a pipeline, a domain, or a reliability metric that's mine to be accountable for. I'd rather be genuinely trusted with one area than superficially involved in five.
questions.evidence: Mirrors how you approached the TfL platform
questions.watchOut: Anchor the learning phase in specifics — lineage, SLAs, what breaks. Generic enthusiasm is forgettable.

questions.question: Why should we hire you?
structure: Name the gap and answer it
questions.answer: Three things. First, I've built and operated production pipelines, not just written them — the freshness improvement at Somalis in Tech was 87%, and holding 95% SLA compliance afterwards was the harder part, because that's about monitoring and incident response rather than the initial build. Second, I've worked both sides of the handoff: nine months as an analyst at HQ Analytics means I know what it's like to consume a badly modelled table, and I build differently because of it. Third, I can explain things — mentoring twelve engineers forces you to justify every decision to someone who'll immediately ask why, and that made my design docs and reviews much sharper. Where I'm honest about the gap: I haven't operated at very large scale or owned a big cloud estate. But my portfolio is mostly me learning production patterns from scratch — Debezium, ClickHouse, dbt, OpenLineage — so the evidence that I close gaps quickly is on the table rather than something you have to take on trust.
questions.evidence: 87% freshness · 95% SLA · 12 mentees · self-taught production stack
questions.watchOut: Naming the gap yourself is what makes the other three claims believable. Do not drop it to sound stronger.

questions.question: What are your salary expectations?
structure: Turn it back into a question
questions.answer: Based on what I've seen for data engineering roles in London at my level, I'm targeting a range of roughly X to Y. That said, I'm flexible depending on the scope of the role, the total package, and what the growth path looks like — if there's a clear route to more ownership, that genuinely matters to me. Is that in line with the band you have for this position?
questions.evidence: Research the current London band before every screen — do not reuse a stale figure
questions.watchOut: Give an actual range. Deflecting entirely reads as unprepared and hands the anchor to them.

questions.question: Do you have any questions for us?
questions.answer: Always yes — three, and never about perks. Ask what the team's biggest data reliability problem is right now, because the answer tells you what the job is actually like day to day and whether they're honest about it. Ask how success is measured at six months, which surfaces whether they've thought about the role or are hiring reactively. Ask what happens when a pipeline breaks — who finds out, who fixes it, whether there's a runbook — because incident culture tells you more about engineering maturity than the stack does. If it's the final round, add one about where the platform is going in the next year, and whether the team is planning to build or buy. And note their answers down; referencing something specific from an earlier round in a later one is one of the cheapest ways to stand out.
questions.evidence: Use in every round · vary by interviewer seniority
questions.watchOut: Have these written down. 'No, I think you covered everything' is a genuinely bad ending.

projects.name: TfL Real-Time Lakehouse
projects.summary: Production-pattern lakehouse ingesting live Transport for London arrival data. Airflow orchestrates ingestion from the TfL API into partitioned Parquet, dbt transforms into analytics-ready marts, Great Expectations validates data quality, and OpenLineage tracks end-to-end lineage via Marquez.
interviewUse: Pipeline architecture: real-time ingestion → raw Parquet → DuckDB silver layer → dbt marts
Data quality: Great Expectations validates nullability, time-to-station bounds at staging
Observability: OpenLineage + Marquez for full lineage tracking
Idempotent design: date-partitioned writes, incremental dbt models

projects.name: TfL Travel App (Somalis in Tech)
projects.summary: Production data engineering project built with Somalis in Tech, born from a student's question: 'How do I actually know when my bus is coming?' Four-layer architecture — Airflow ingests from TfL Unified API every 3 minutes into date/hour-partitioned Parquet, dbt transforms through staging → intermediate → marts (medallion pattern), Great Expectations validates quality, and OpenLineage tracks lineage. Features real-time arrival predictions, line disruption alerts, and historical reliability patterns. Improved data freshness from 6 hours to 45 minutes (87%), reduced manual reporting by 65%, and served as a teaching platform for ~12 early-career engineers via the Caawi Mentorship Platform.
interviewUse: Origin story: a student asked 'How do I know when my bus is coming?' — identified a real gap in how TfL data served commuters
Four-layer architecture: ingestion (Airflow, 3-min polling) → storage (Parquet, date/hour partitioned) → transformation (dbt medallion) → quality (Great Expectations + OpenLineage)
API rate limiting solved with priority-based polling: high-traffic stops refresh more frequently, graceful degradation to cached data when limits hit
Schema evolution handled defensively: raw layer stores unmodified responses, staging uses explicit column selection, dbt tests catch breaks before downstream propagation
Modularity: designed so DuckDB can swap for BigQuery, local Parquet for S3 — config changes only, no rewrites
Three data products: real-time arrival predictions, line disruption alerts, historical reliability patterns (students said this was most valuable)
Mentorship: taught 12 candidates across 4 modules — API ingestion, data modelling, data quality, pipeline orchestration
Impact: 87% freshness improvement, 65% manual reporting reduction, mentees went on to build their own lakehouses
Key insight: 'The gap between it works and it helps is the difference between engineering and software worth building'
